query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying an aluminide-based surface coating to cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will form a protective Al2O3 scale that significantly improves its oxygen resistance at high temperatures without degrading its intrinsic tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C (strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1), but with poor oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Apply a thin, uniform aluminide coating (e.g., via pack cementation or atomic layer deposition) that converts into a stable, adherent alumina (Al2O3) scale upon high-temperature exposure.
generation.conditions: Expose coated samples to air at 1000 °C for approximately 100 hours under conditions mimicking service thermal cycles, while subjecting them to comparable mechanical loading rates as the untreated baseline.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 scale that serves as a diffusion barrier to oxygen.
generation.mechanism: The aluminide coating reacts at high temperature to form a protective alumina layer that prevents oxygen ingress, thereby significantly reducing oxidation without altering the alloy’s underlying microstructure which governs its mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coated HfNbTaTiZr samples will exhibit markedly reduced oxidation (lower weight gain and oxide scale thickness) at 1000 °C, while retaining similar room-temperature ductility (8–16%) and high-temperature yield strength (within the 163–530 MPa range) compared to untreated samples.
generation.baseline: Untreated cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr that suffers from poor oxygen resistance despite its otherwise useful mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold under high-temperature exposure (around 1000 °C) in air for durations on the order of 100 hours and mechanical tests performed at strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1; deviations in coating performance under more extreme conditions remain unverified.
generation.uncertainty: The long-term adhesion and integrity of the alumina scale during cyclic thermal-mechanical loading are uncertain, as are potential impacts of the coating process on near-surface microstructure.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical cast HfNbTaTiZr specimens and subject half to an aluminide coating process while leaving the other half uncoated. Expose both groups to a 100-hour oxidation test in air at 1000 °C, then perform both room temperature and high-temperature tensile tests.
measurements: Weight gain measurements during oxidation exposure
Surface oxide scale characterization (using SEM/EDS and XRD) to confirm formation and integrity of the alumina scale
High-temperature tensile tests to determine yield strength
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated specimens show a significant reduction in oxidation (i.e., lower weight gain and a consistent, adherent alumina scale) while maintaining tensile properties within the baseline range, the hypothesis is supported; if the coating degrades, fails to form a protective layer, or if mechanical properties deteriorate relative to the uncoated control, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on Mechanical Properties of Equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr Alloys

Abstract: AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect

Conclusions: The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen
